explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. "For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob like the splendor of Israel…" (Nahum 2:2). Destroyers had laid them waste and ruined the branches of their vine, and the LORD says He will restore them anyway. Right in the middle of a loud, scary scene, Nahum slips in a promise.

The fortress is in verse 1, friend, but that call is aimed at Nineveh: "Guard the fortress!" (Nahum 2:1). For Jacob, Nahum says something else. "For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob…" (Nahum 2:2). The promise is restoration, not hiding.

No king shows up in this verse, friend. Nahum says, "For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob like the splendor of Israel…" (Nahum 2:2). Destroyers had ruined the branches of their vine, so the promise is about their splendor coming back. I think that's a good thing to carry out of this verse.

Torches, friend! The chariots "appear like torches, darting about like lightning" (Nahum 2:4). They dash through the streets and rush around the plazas. I'd hate to be the one standing in a crosswalk there.
Clouds drift, friend, and these chariots do not drift. They dash through the streets and rush around the plazas. Nahum says they appear like torches and dart about like lightning (Nahum 2:4).
Shadows stay quiet and sneak around, but this scene is loud and bright. The chariots are "appearing like torches, darting about like lightning" (Nahum 2:4). Nothing in that picture is trying to hide.
True! "The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses" (Nahum 2:6). Nahum says it in one short sentence, and I think that makes it hit harder. The gates open, and the palace falls.

It's actually true, friend. Nahum says, "The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses" (Nahum 2:6). The gates open and the palace falls, all in one short line. I know it's a lot to picture.

explanations.answer: That it be exiled and carried away
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. "It is decreed that the city be exiled and carried away…" (Nahum 2:7). The palace has fallen, and now the city itself is carried off. I think that's a big change for a city that felt so settled.

explanations.answer: That it pay a yearly tribute
explanations.explanation: A yearly payment would mean the city stays put and keeps going, friend. That's not what Nahum says. "It is decreed that the city be exiled and carried away…" (Nahum 2:7). This city is being carried off.

explanations.answer: That it be rebuilt in stone
explanations.explanation: Nobody is building anything in this verse, friend. The palace has just collapsed, and the decree is that the city "be exiled and carried away" (Nahum 2:7). Rebuilding isn't mentioned. I think a city that's being carried off isn't thinking about stonework.

Draining away, friend. "Nineveh has been like a pool of water throughout her days, but now it is draining away" (Nahum 2:8). A pool that has sat there for ages is emptying out. I think that's a picture you can see without any help.
Freezing would hold the water in place, friend, and Nahum says the opposite. The pool "is draining away" (Nahum 2:8). Nothing is staying put.

Nahum says nothing about the taste of this pool, friend. He says, "Nineveh has been like a pool of water throughout her days, but now it is draining away" (Nahum 2:8). It isn't changing flavor. It's running out.
True. "'Stop! Stop!' they cry, but no one turns back" (Nahum 2:8). People are calling out for it to stop, and nobody turns around. I think that's a sad scene.
That one's true, friend. Nahum says, "'Stop! Stop!' they cry, but no one turns back" (Nahum 2:8). The cry goes out as the pool drains. Nobody turns around.

I see why you'd pick it, friend, but the text says otherwise. Nahum says, "There is no end to the treasure, an abundance of every precious thing" (Nahum 2:9). The plunderers keep grabbing silver and gold, and the treasure doesn't run out. That's why the answer is False.

False is right! Nahum says, "There is no end to the treasure, an abundance of every precious thing" (Nahum 2:9). They keep shouting, "Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!" and the pile doesn't run out. Even with all that grabbing, they never get to the bottom of it.
Yes, friend. "She is emptied! Yes, she is desolate and laid waste!" (Nahum 2:10). After all that plundering, the city is left bare. Nahum puts it plainly.

That would be Nineveh before the plundering, friend. Nahum says there was "an abundance of every precious thing" (Nahum 2:9), but then he says, "She is emptied! Yes, she is desolate and laid waste!" (Nahum 2:10). The riches are gone, and no pride is mentioned.

It may be quiet, friend, but it's not peaceful. Nahum says, "Hearts melt, knees knock, bodies tremble, and every face grows pale!" (Nahum 2:10). He calls the city "desolate and laid waste." I think peace is the last word for that.
True! "Hearts melt, knees knock, bodies tremble, and every face grows pale!" (Nahum 2:10). Nahum piles one reaction on another. I think anybody would know that feeling.

That one's true, friend. Nahum says, "Hearts melt, knees knock, bodies tremble, and every face grows pale!" (Nahum 2:10). Knees knocking and pale faces are both in the verse. He lists them one after another.

That's right, friend. "The lion mauled enough for its cubs and strangled prey for the lioness. It filled its dens with the kill, and its lairs with mauled prey" (Nahum 2:12). It's a picture of a lion that never comes home short. I think it's heavy, so I'll say it once and move on.

Nahum paints this lion as doing far better than that, friend. He says, "The lion mauled enough for its cubs and strangled prey for the lioness" (Nahum 2:12). The text says it filled its dens, which is more than getting by.
This lion doesn't come home with little, friend. Nahum says, "It filled its dens with the kill, and its lairs with mauled prey" (Nahum 2:12). The dens are full, not empty.

Against, friend. "Behold, I am against you," declares the LORD of Hosts (Nahum 2:13). The LORD speaks plainly, and there's no way to misread it. After all the pictures in this chapter, here is His own voice.
"With" is a comforting word, friend, but it isn't the one here. The LORD of Hosts says, "Behold, I am against you" (Nahum 2:13). He is speaking to Nineveh, and He says He is against her.
The LORD doesn't talk about distance in this verse, friend. He says, "Behold, I am against you," declares the LORD of Hosts (Nahum 2:13). The word is "against," and it's hard to miss.
That's it, friend. The LORD says, "…the voices of your messengers will no longer be heard" (Nahum 2:13). He says it last, after the chariots, the young lions and the prey. Those voices go quiet.
Songs aren't in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "…the voices of your messengers will no longer be heard" (Nahum 2:13). Temples don't come up at all in what He says.

The LORD does talk about chariots and the sword in this verse, friend, but the roar of armies isn't what goes silent. He says, "…the voices of your messengers will no longer be heard" (Nahum 2:13). It's the messengers' voices that He names.
